note: AI-authored original IELTS Academic Reading passage for the morning-quiz bank (2026-07, batch v2). Not from a past examination paper. Factual content on stratospheric ozone depletion, CFCs, the Molina-Rowland chlorine catalysis, the Antarctic ozone hole (Farman et al. 1985), the 1987 Montreal Protocol, the 2016 Kigali Amendment, and projected recovery (WMO/UNEP 2022 assessment). ~775 words; 13 questions across matching-information, TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN, sentence completion and flow-chart completion.
passage:
Paragraph A
In the middle of the 1980s a group of scientists working in Antarctica made an alarming discovery. Each spring, a vast region of the atmosphere above the frozen continent was losing much of its ozone, the gas that shields the Earth from the harsher part of the sun's light. Their measurements revealed a thinning so severe that it soon became known around the world as the ozone hole. For years the layer had been quietly monitored, yet nothing had prepared the researchers for a gap so large that at first they suspected their own instruments were faulty. The finding turned a little-understood corner of chemistry into one of the defining environmental stories of the century.

Paragraph B
Ozone is a form of oxygen that gathers in the stratosphere, the calm layer of air that begins roughly ten kilometres above our heads. There it performs a service on which life on land depends: it absorbs most of the sun's ultraviolet radiation, the invisible, high-energy light that harms living tissue. If that shield were to weaken, doctors warned, rates of skin cancer and eye cataracts would rise, and the delicate plankton at the base of the ocean food chain, along with many crops, would begin to suffer.

Paragraph C
The threat came from a family of manufactured chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs. First produced in the 1930s and long celebrated as a triumph of industrial chemistry, they were valued precisely because they were so unreactive and safe to handle. Cheap, stable and non-poisonous, they had spread through modern life within a few decades of their invention. They were the standard cooling fluid in refrigerators and air conditioners, the propellant that pushed paint and hairspray out of aerosol cans, and the gas used to blow the bubbles in plastic foams. Their great virtue was also their hidden danger: because CFCs do not break down near the ground, they simply drift upward, year after year, until they reach the stratosphere.

Paragraph D
There, struck by the full force of the sun's ultraviolet light, the CFC molecules finally shatter and release chlorine. In 1974 two chemists, Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland, worked out what happens next. A single atom of chlorine, they showed, behaves as a catalyst: it destroys one ozone molecule after another, thousands of them in turn, without ever being used up itself. The damage is worst over Antarctica, because clouds that form only in the bitter cold of the polar winter speed up the reactions, so that when the spring sunlight returns a great hole opens in the ozone above the continent.

Paragraph E
The world's response was unusually swift and united. In 1987 governments met and signed the Montreal Protocol, a treaty committing them to phase out the production of CFCs. In the years that followed the agreement was repeatedly tightened as the science grew clearer, and it was eventually ratified by every single country on Earth — the first treaty in the history of the United Nations to win such complete support. Factories switched to new chemicals, and the output of CFCs fell steeply.

Paragraph F
Replacing the banned chemicals proved to be complicated. The first substitutes still contained some chlorine, and the next generation, though far kinder to the ozone layer, turned out to be powerful greenhouse gases that trap heat in the lower atmosphere. To close this loophole, a further deal, the Kigali Amendment of 2016, committed nations to reducing these replacement gases too, tying the repair of the ozone layer directly to the broader struggle against climate change.

Paragraph G
The effort is working, but it is slow. Because the CFCs already released will linger in the air for decades, the ozone layer cannot heal overnight. Careful measurements show that the Antarctic hole is, on average, gradually shrinking. Scientists now expect ozone over most of the planet to return to its 1980 condition around the middle of this century, with the Antarctic region, where the loss was greatest, recovering a decade or two later than the rest. This slow recovery is tracked by satellites overhead and by instruments carried aloft on balloons launched from research stations scattered across the globe.

Paragraph H
The ozone story is often held up as the most successful environmental agreement ever reached. It has quietly done a second job as well, for many of the banned chemicals were greenhouse gases, and phasing them out has spared the planet a large amount of additional warming. Above all, it showed that when the evidence is clear and nations are willing to act together, even a threat spread across the whole sky can be turned back — a lesson that those now facing climate change return to again and again.
